## Project overview

This experiment examined whether oil type and the timing of adding popcorn
kernels affect total popping time. The study compared olive, vegetable, and
coconut oil under two starting procedures. It was designed to distinguish the
effects of each factor and determine whether the effect of kernel timing varied
by oil type.

> **Key finding:** The report concluded that the heated-start procedure took
> longer than the cold-start procedure (*p* = 0.00441). Oil type and the
> interaction between oil type and kernel timing were not statistically
> significant at the 0.05 level.

## Study design

The team used a balanced, randomized 2 × 3 factorial design:

| Factor | Conditions |
| --- | --- |
| Oil type | Olive, vegetable, and coconut |
| Kernel timing | Cold start and heated start |

Each of the six treatment combinations was repeated five times, for 30 trials
in total. The response variable was the time to complete popping, measured in
seconds. Treatment order was randomized before data collection to reduce
potential bias from trial order.

For a cold-start trial, the kernels were added to the oil at the beginning of
heating. For a heated-start trial, four kernels were added first; the remaining
kernels were added after the first of those kernels popped. Trials followed a
consistent stovetop procedure, including a standard oil amount, medium-high
heat, and a defined stopping point based on the interval between pops.

## Analysis and results

A two-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) was used to evaluate the effects of oil
type, kernel timing, and their interaction on total popping time. At a
significance level of α = 0.05, the results were:

| Effect | *p*-value | Interpretation |
| --- | ---: | --- |
| Kernel timing | 0.00441 | Statistically significant |
| Oil type | 0.06552 | Not statistically significant |
| Oil type × kernel timing | 0.09184 | Not statistically significant |

The report concluded that the heated-start procedure took longer than the
cold-start procedure. The study did not find sufficient evidence that popping
time differed by oil type, or that the effect of kernel timing depended on the
oil used. These non-significant findings do not establish that the effects are
exactly zero.

The team reviewed residual diagnostic plots and reported that the residuals
were approximately normal, the randomized order supported independence, and
the spread across groups was sufficiently similar for the equal-variance
assumption to be reasonable. A log transformation was considered but did not
improve the residual spread, so the untransformed model was retained. The
reported power calculation, based on the observed data, exceeded 90%.

## Interpretation and limitations

Because treatment order was randomized and the procedure was controlled, the
results support causal conclusions for this specific stovetop setup. They
should not be generalized to all popcorn, cooking equipment, or heating
conditions. Differences in burner temperature, pan cooldown, and other
uncontrolled aspects of the setup may have contributed to variation between
trials.

Further work could use temperature-controlled equipment, allow more time
between trials, increase the number of replications, and examine additional
outcomes such as unpopped kernels, popped volume, or burning.
